extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York; citizens/voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution (general public interested in constitutional powers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate the powers conferred by the proposed U.S. Constitution: whether each power is necessary, properly limited, and how it compares to the defects of the Articles of Confederation. The page is a Federalist essay arguing what powers the federal government should have and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess quantity and danger of vested powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether any part of the powers transferred to the general government is unnecessary or improper, and whether the aggregate of them is dangerous to the portion of jurisdiction left to the several States; i.e., is the aggregate power greater than ought to have been vested in it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review powers relative to their necessity as means to ends. Avoid dwelling only on possible inconveniences or abuses; instead ask whether a power is necessary to achieve a legitimate public good, and if so, how to guard against perversion or abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity principle for conferring power
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases where power is to be conferred, the first point to be decided is whether such a power be necessary to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge powers by whether they are necessary means to attain necessary ends. If a power is necessary, then focus on designing safeguards to prevent its abuse rather than rejecting it simply because abuses are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against perversion of necessary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is affirmed that a power is necessary, the next point is to guard as effectually as possible against a perversion of the power to the public detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional restraints, terms, and institutional checks (e.g., appropriations limits, elections) to minimize risk of abuse. Consider whether the instrument contains explicit limitations and enumerations that constrain broad language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of federal powers for review
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers may be usefully reduced into classes tied to objects: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony among the States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of States from injurious acts; (6) provisions for giving due efficacy to these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy as a checklist when surveying constitutional powers so no relevant functional area is overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to declare war and grant letters of marque
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to declare war and grant letters of marque is necessary as a fundamental attribute for security against foreign danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat declaration-of-war power as non-controversial necessity; it's consistent with the Confederation and essential for national defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to raise armies and maintain fleets (including in peacetime)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of raising armies and equipping fleets is involved in self-defense, and includes the question whether an indefinite power to raise troops and to maintain them in peace as well as war is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that preparedness (including peacetime establishments) cannot be safely prohibited if other nations maintain forces. Limiting the force of defense while not limiting others' offensive capabilities is impractical and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on standing armies via appropriations terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the term for which revenue may be appropriated to standing forces (e.g., Constitution's two-year limit) is a prudent precaution against danger from standing armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare institutional mechanisms (annual vs. multi-year appropriations) in context; short appropriation terms tied to frequent elections reduce risk of permanent military establishments. Beware fallacious comparisons that ignore parliamentary differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as safeguard against dangerous standing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: A united America, even with few troops, is a better deterrent to foreign ambition than disunited States with large standing armies; union reduces the need for dangerous peace establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider structural effects (union vs. disunion) on military needs—political arrangements can reduce necessity for large standing forces and thereby protect liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide and maintain a navy
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to provide and maintain a navy is necessary and is among the greatest safeguards of the nation, particularly for maritime frontiers and commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat naval power as less likely to be used against liberties (batteries defending coasts) and essential for protecting commerce; states exposed to maritime danger have special interest in federal naval powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to levy and borrow money for common defense and welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to levy and borrow money is the sinew of national defense and is necessary both in its extent and form as given by the Constitution; revenue sources cannot be confined solely to external taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate demographic/economic changes that shift revenue bases (imports decrease as domestic manufactures grow); a durable government must have flexible taxation powers. Resist narrow constructions that would handicap future revenue needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper construction of general welfare taxation clause
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'to lay and collect taxes ... to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare' does not amount to an unlimited commission to exercise every power; it must be read in light of the subsequent enumeration of particular powers which explain and qualify the general phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret general grants in the context of enumerated powers; avoid construing a general clause as swallowing specific limitations. Use textual rules: general phrase followed by specific recital usually means specifics qualify the general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power over treaties, ambassadors, and consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors and other public ministers or consuls is properly a federal power for coherent national conduct toward other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure treaty power isn't frustrated by state regulations; extend appointment power beyond 'ambassador' to include lower grades and consuls when necessary for practical diplomacy and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to define and punish piracies, felonies on the high seas, and offenses against law of nations
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal power to define and punish piracies, felonies on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations is appropriate and necessary for uniformity and to prevent a single state embroiling the Confederacy with foreign nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative definitions are needed for certainty and uniformity because common law and state statutes vary; avoid leaving such definitions to disparate state laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of foreign commerce (including prohibition of slave importation after 1808)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to regulate foreign commerce is essential; includes a power to prohibit importation of slaves (deferred until 1808) and to impose duties; this power is a significant improvement over the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both practical and moral dimensions; while ideally prohibitions might be immediate, a time-limited postponement is a political compromise that still advances the humanitarian goal over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate commerce among the States to prevent burdensome tolls and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to regulate commerce among the several States prevents states from imposing duties or tolls on goods passing through their jurisdictions that would burden other states' trade and incite animosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal supervision of interstate commerce is necessary to prevent retaliation, economic friction, and interruptions of public tranquility; evidence from other confederacies (Switzerland, Germany, Netherlands) illustrates risks of weak supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate commerce with Indian tribes free of confusing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to regulate commerce with Indian tribes should be unfettered by the confusing and contradictory limits present in the Articles of Confederation (e.g., 'Indians not members of any of the States').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous qualifications that leave jurisdictional confusion over which Indians are 'members' of states; federal authority avoids contradictory state intrusions and practical impossibilities under the Confederation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to coin money and regulate value of domestic and foreign coin
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal authority to coin money and regulate its value, including that of foreign coin, is necessary to secure uniformity in currency value across the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level variation in treatment of foreign coin could destroy uniform value; federal regulation prevents states from undermining monetary uniformity that commerce depends on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to punish counterfeiting of coins and public securities
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation should include the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and the securities of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign this to the federal authority that secures the value of coin and public securities to ensure uniform criminal treatment and preserve financial integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to fix the standard of weights and measures is transferred to the federal government to ensure uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform standards are necessary for commerce and legal certainty; federal control prevents state-by-state divergence that would complicate trade and contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a uniform rule of naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution should authorize the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States to avoid conflicting state rules and absurd consequences of varying definitions of citizenship or 'inhabitants'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A uniform rule prevents a person being a citizen in one state but excluded in another, eliminates forum-shopping by aliens seeking easier naturalization, and avoids strange legal collisions (e.g., proscribed persons gaining citizenship elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish uniform laws of bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy is intimately connected with regulation of commerce and will prevent many frauds where parties or property may lie or be removed into different States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform bankruptcy laws reduce cross-border fraud and uncertainty and are an essential complement to interstate commerce regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide rules for public acts, records, judicial proceedings across states; postal infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution contemplates provisions to prescribe how public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved and what effect they shall have in other States, and to establish post offices and post roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures give 'due efficacy' to federal powers: ensure interstate recognition of official acts and a communication/postal network necessary for national administration and commerce.
